correctness.rationale: For selected counts \(s_i\), omitted demands \(t_i=n-s_i\), and same-part pair capacities \(p_i=\binom{s_i}{2}\), shortest-path coverage is exactly a three-class bipartite allocation problem. Hall reduces to \(T\le P\) and \(t_i\le P-p_i\) for all three classes, because any demand subset meeting two partite classes sees all three pair-slot classes. The displayed inequalities then prove that \((2,2,n-2)\) is minimal strong geodetic and that every larger strong set admits a one-vertex deletion; the equality argument leaves only \((2,2,n-2)\). I independently reimplemented the Hall criterion and one-vertex minimality test, recovering the stated value and exactly three maximum patterns at every tested stable-range value, including \(n=12,13,14,15,20,30,40\). The packaged max-flow verifier was read and exhaustively checks all part-count triples for \(12\le n\le30\); finite checks are corroborative only.
correctness.risk: The theorem is a stable-range result and does not classify \(n<12\) or unbalanced tripartite graphs.

value.rationale: Passing from two to three partite classes changes the covering problem into a genuine three-class allocation system. The theorem gives an infinite stable exact value, a full structural classification of extremal minimal sets, and an exact count, which is a natural benchmark for the upper geodetic parameter.
value.risk: The stable threshold is not claimed optimal for every possible structural property below \(n=12\).

final_claim: For every integer \(n\ge12\), the strong upper geodetic number of \(K_{n,n,n}\) is \(n+2\); maximum minimal strong geodetic sets have exactly the three part-count patterns obtained by permuting \((2,2,n-2)\), giving \(3\binom n2^3\) such sets.
limitations: Finite max-flow computations are corroborative, not the infinite proof.
